answer.rationale: The binding constraints are supply continuity (contract lapses in 14 days, line at 94% with no buffer) and an 18% cost mandate. A full primary-vendor switch is the only memory that promises a sharp unit-cost cut (memory_c2), but executing a migration inside 14 days at 94% utilization directly violates the 'without increasing delivery risk' half of the objective, so I will not lead with it. add_second_source (memory_c3) is the right resilience move but is slow to qualify and does not by itself deliver an 18% in-year cut; defer_decision (memory_c5) applied to a critical, non-auto-renewing primary contract is category error 	a non-critical service, not the line's feedstock. That leaves the incumbent. Price is closed this cycle by the incumbent's own statement, which neutralizes the straightforward benchmarking play in memory_c4 	but memory_c6 describes a structurally different lever: term length and volume commitment rather than reopening the current price sheet. That is why I am verifying memory_c6 first 	I need to know whether the volume pricing was genuinely a term-structure concession, at comparable spend and on this component class, or whether it was really just a renegotiation under a different label, in which case the refusal kills it too. I am verifying memory_c2 second because it is the fallback and the largest claimed saving, and 'onboarding was quick' is exactly the kind of compressed outcome statement that hides the ramp duration, the component's criticality, and whether the line had buffer at the time. Caution on the memory set as a whole: all six entries record a success and none records a failure or a base rate, which is a survivorship pattern; each is an outcome summary stripped of the conditions that produced it, and the two most cost-relevant ones (c2, c6) date from a period with slack that does not exist now. I am treating them as leads to be re-grounded, not as settled policy. If verification shows the multi-year lever is real, I commit to a term-restructured renewal that books the cost reduction while preserving continuity, and I queue second-sourcing for the next review. If it shows the lever was price renegotiation in disguise, I fall back to a continuity-first renewal and carry the cost gap explicitly to finance rather than absorbing migration risk on a line with no buffer.
